cards.title: Only trust ads you can trace
cards.summary: Judge every ad, creative choice and offer by keyed returns, never by opinion or imitation of untraced advertising.
cards.use_when: Choosing ad creative, headlines or offers for any campaign and deciding whose advice to follow.
steps: Key every ad so you can attribute replies, coupons, codes or store presentations to a specific ad, headline, plan or method.
Treat any ad that produces no traced result as unproven; refuse to copy a competitor's ad or follow an advertiser's style unless you know its measured returns.
Ignore opinions from anyone who cannot show their returns, including colleagues, printers and self-described experts; test their suggestions instead.
Note that brief, cryptic ads are almost never keyed — assume they were never measured, not that they work.
Accept that full, story-telling ads are the norm in traced mail-order advertising because long copy can be tracked and attributed.
Base changes to your creative on compared results, not on arguments around a table.
caveats: This is Hopkins' 1923 position; modern platforms give partial attribution and modelled conversions, so treat keyed data as directional for upper-funnel spend.
Some brand-building spend cannot be cleanly keyed; don't conclude it does nothing, only that you cannot yet price it.

cards.title: Make your product its own best salesman with samples
cards.summary: Use samples not as giveaways but as interest filters that generate keyed prospects, cheaper follow-up and a fair product test.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether and how to run a sampling or trial offer for a physical product before scaling acquisition.
steps: Offer a sample so you can legitimately use the word 'Free', which the source says typically multiplies readers and can repay the sample cost several times over in extra attention.
Require effort before fulfilment — a cut-out coupon, phone call or store visit — so only interested prospects receive samples.
Never distribute samples promiscuously to homes or hand stocks to dealers to give away; the source says such samples cheapen the product and often never reach the buyer.
Samples and coupons both register interest, so use them to key and compare one ad, headline or plan against another.
Where international or out-of-area circulation would waste coupons, tell those readers to write for a sample and then route them to a local stockist.
Where offered, price at full-size package rather than half-price: before a prospect is converted, getting half price is about as hard as getting full price.
caveats: The source's numeric examples (costs of 15–70 cents per inquiry, fourfold response to store presentation) are dated mail-order figures, not current benchmarks.
Repeaters from sampling are a small percentage; Hopkins says the loss is usually smaller than the cost of policing it.

cards.title: Deliver samples where people already shop
cards.summary: Local sample delivery at stores drastically reduces inquiry cost versus mail, and simultaneously builds distribution.
cards.use_when: Structuring a sample or coupon offer and choosing between mail fulfilment, phone response and local store redemption.
steps: Prefer coupons presented at a local store over mailed coupons; Hopkins reports the same ads bringing inquiries at 18–22 cents versus 70 cents by mail.
Offer multiple response routes where practical; in one case 70% of inquiries came by telephone rather than mail, because writing and stamps are a barrier.
If a newspaper's circulation reaches outside towns, tell those readers to write while routing local readers to stores — mailing a sample may convert someone who cannot then be supplied.
Have participating dealers return coupons promptly so you can follow up while interest is fresh.
Require a stock purchase to receive samples if only some stores can be supplied (e.g. a dozen samples with a dozen packages), then refer all inquiries to those stores.
Say 'only one sample to a home' and 'adults only' where children or hoarding would waste samples.
caveats: Some buyers or dealers may buy up papers for full-size-package coupons; the source advises not announcing the offer date and using Sunday papers.
Store demonstrations and promiscuous handouts are called out as poor use of samples unless interest is established first.

cards.title: Use test campaigns to answer selling questions before you scale
cards.summary: Prove a new product, form, price or method in a few towns, measure cost and repeat purchase, then roll out with known economics.
cards.use_when: Launching a new product, new campaign or major creative change, or deciding whether to scale national spend.
steps: Pick four or five average towns (or other representative test cells) rather than relying on the opinions of you and your advisers.
Run the offer with a sample or free package to start users quickly, then measure: do they buy, do they repeat, how much do they buy, and how long until profit repays selling cost.
Compute cost per customer and revenue per customer from the test; Hopkins asserts averages from a small scale reliably predict the large scale.
Use the test to try alternative product forms; one advertiser found near-unanimous disapproval of a planned reformulation and 91% approval of a second form.
Use tests to try new methods on an already-successful campaign, without disturbing the running campaign; one food advertiser tried over 50 plans in five years and eventually cut selling cost 75%.
Let a challenger prove superior skill by running a few towns and comparing cost per result with the incumbent campaign.
caveats: Hopkins cites typical test costs of $1,000–$5,000; these are 1920s figures, and the general method — not the numbers — is the transferable part.
The dollar amounts and the 75% improvement are case examples, not promised results.

cards.title: Judge a product by whether repeat sales repay acquisition cost
cards.summary: Before scaling, establish cost per customer, revenue per customer and payback time; short-lived, one-purchase items often can't be advertised profitably.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to advertise a new product, setting allowable acquisition cost, or comparing products for portfolio investment.
steps: Learn what a user spends per year, total consumption in the market and the percentage of readers the product appeals to — waste circulation drives cost.
Compute cost per customer from keyed tests rather than guesswork, and check whether purchases repeat and at what interval.

For single-purchase articles, assume acquisition cost roughly matches mail-order costs for comparable single items; Hopkins says mail-order sales on single articles rarely cost less than $2.50 each, and dealer-sold equivalents cost about as much.

Reject claims aimed at prevention rather than cure: Hopkins says people will pay a lot to cure trouble but little to prevent it, and a prevention claim may pull far less than an alternative benefit claim.
Ask whether the product lasts too long or appeals to too small a percentage, in which case most spend reaches non-buyers.
Project payback: if the ad cost returns before bills are due, the product can be advertised without investment; if it takes months, finance accordingly.
caveats: Numeric thresholds are 1923 US mail-order figures and should not be applied literally today.
Repeat-purchase rates and appeal percentages vary by line and must be measured for your own product.

cards.title: Don't spend to educate a habit you can't own
cards.summary: Changing consumer habits is prohibitive for one advertiser; watch trends created by others and move in to satisfy demand at the right time.
cards.use_when: Evaluating a campaign that tries to create a new consumer habit, category or education objective rather than satisfy existing demand.
steps: Estimate the cost of converting non-users; Hopkins cites a dentifrice case where converts cost $20–$25 each, making the spend unrecoverable in a lifetime of sales.

If a habit change is needed to use your product, consider abandoning the education objective entirely rather than allocating a share of each ad to it — Hopkins calls partial funding 'the same folly on a smaller scale.'
Prefer satisfying already-created wants: monitor popular trends, fashions and newly created desires, then offer to satisfy them when demand appears (he cites yeast and antiseptics).
Consider shared category education only through cooperative funding across many producers, since no single advertiser can recoup the cost alone.
Check that your ad reaches newly converted buyers rather than re-educating people who already use the category.
caveats: Hopkins' cost figures are 1920s and line-specific; the principle — calculate convert cost before funding education — is what transfers.
Some modern brands do profitably create categories, but typically with capital, long horizons or shared spend.

cards.title: Pick the claim that appeals to the most buyers
cards.summary: When a product has several true claims, feature the one with the widest appeal in headlines and relegate niche claims to body copy or occasional ads.
cards.use_when: Writing headlines and PDP copy for a product with multiple benefits, especially health, cosmetic or functional claims.
steps: List every true claim the product supports, then estimate what percentage of buyers each appeals to.

Feature the broadest, most attractive claim in headlines; Hopkins reports a toothpaste that prevents decay but also beautifies teeth succeeded by never featuring tooth trouble, while competitors centering on trouble pulled less.
Avoid letting a narrow claim contaminate a broad one: he says mentioning an eczema claim on a soap might destroy the beauty claim that appeals to nearly all buyers.
For claims appealing to roughly a quarter of customers, include them in a percentage of ads and probably in every ad's body copy, but don't make them the headline.
Test headlines against each other with keyed returns; Hopkins says one heading may pull ten times another, so guessing is unsafe.
Use exactness to strengthen a claim: instead of 'good food value,' state the laboratory figure (e.g. 425 calories per pint, equal to six eggs).
caveats: Appeal percentages must be measured for your product; the source's examples are illustrations, not benchmarks.
Some regulated categories restrict comparative or health claims; verify current rules before publishing.

cards.title: Research the product exhaustively before writing
cards.summary: Weeks of reading, consumer canvassing and dealer research often surface the single fact that becomes the campaign's keystone.
cards.use_when: Preparing to write ad or PDP copy for a new product or entering a category you don't know well.
steps: Read widely in the product's technical or scientific literature; Hopkins describes weeks of medical reading on coffee that yielded one fact — caffeine's stimulation comes two hours after drinking — which reframed a caffeine-free coffee from a near-beer substitute into a full-pleasure product.

Interview consumers at scale: canvasses of all classes, thousands of home interviews and questionnaires to tens of thousands of prospects are the source's norm before a food or personal-care campaign.
Survey dealers and gather every rival's literature, claims and current advertising so you start with exact knowledge of what competitors are saying.

Count the addressable base before choosing the appeal: one pork-and-beans canvass found only 4% used canned beans, so the winning approach targeted home bakers rather than the 4% brand-choice minority.
Employ chemists or labs to verify or disprove claims; Hopkins warns that an untrue impressive assertion can bar you from good media and damage credibility.
Apply the same research approach to existing products when launching a new line or reformulation, not just new brands.
caveats: Research volume must fit the margin available on the product and the size of the opportunity.
Some canvass figures in the source are decades old; the practice of primary research, not the specific percentages, transfers.

cards.title: Choose names and prices as strategy, not afterthoughts
cards.summary: Names that tell a story or create an exclusive category, and prices matched to volume versus margin needs, shape an entire campaign.
cards.use_when: Naming a product or line extension, and setting or repositioning price before advertising.
steps: For a name, weigh descriptive names that tell a story (Shredded Wheat, Cream of Wheat, Puffed Rice) against coined names that can become category names (Kodak, Karo, Jell-O, Vaseline) and prevent substitution.

Prefer a coined or owned name over a generic descriptor: Hopkins says Toasted Corn Flakes and Horlick's Malted Milk left the way open to perpetual substitution and lost much of the market they pioneered.
When setting price, decide between high volume at thin margin (Campbell's Soup, Palmolive, Ford) and high margin with small consumption per customer (a corn remedy used rarely).
Recognize that a high price can itself be an inducement where products are judged by price and buyers assume expensive means better.
Note that a price appealing to only about 10% of buyers multiplies the cost of selling by narrowing the field.
Check that the price leaves enough margin to fund the advertising required for the volume you need.
caveats: These are Hopkins' 1923 examples; subscription, SaaS and marketplace economics differ.
High-price-as-quality only works in categories where buyers use price as a quality signal.

cards.title: Map the competitive field before choosing your angle
cards.summary: Study entrenched rivals' price, quality and claims, and find a real, tellable advantage that gives satisfied users a reason to switch.
cards.use_when: Entering an established category or launching against entrenched brands, and deciding whether to attack, differentiate or avoid the fight.
steps: Inventory the forces against you: rivals' prices, quality levels, claims and how strongly they are entrenched, including whether they created and typify the habit.
Accept that fields where one brand originated and typifies a habit are nearly impregnable; invasion requires a convincing advantage or superior sales copy, not a comparable product and a budget.

Work through substitution mechanics: for a new shaving soap, every prospect uses a rival and many are satisfied, so describe the individual — a man on a Pullman with his favourite soap — and determine what you could say to him personally to make him switch.
Win one specific customer type first: 'We cannot go after thousands of men until we learn how to win one.'
If the maker claims no distinction, hunt for an impressive fact about the product that competitors have not told; it doesn't need to be unique, only more convincing.
Plan defences against substitution from the start; a brand that only establishes a demand, without owning the name or claim, may lose the harvest it created.
caveats: Head-on attacks on habit-creating leaders usually fail regardless of copy quality.
The source's case is about physical goods sold through dealers; marketplaces and marketplaces-with-reviews face additional trust factors.

cards.title: Get distribution before or alongside advertising
cards.summary: Advertising before availability wastes converts; use sample and coupon offers naming specific dealers to force stock and achieve distribution quickly.
cards.use_when: Running any campaign where consumers must be able to buy immediately after seeing the ad.
steps: Choose a distribution method — direct/mail order until volume forces retailers, referral of inquirers to stocked dealers, consignment to wholesalers, or named-dealer advertising — based on your line.
Start locally, naming specific dealers in the first ads; when other dealers see rivals named, they typically stock quickly if advertising pulls.

Use coupons good at any store for a full-size package: mail proofs of the ad to dealers in advance with a list of media and circulation, so each dealer sees coupon holders as cash sales they don't want to lose.
Where samples are used, supply participating stores with samples in proportion to a stock purchase, then refer inquiries to all stores to force general distribution.
Avoid sending free stock or starting with consignment as default methods; Hopkins calls free starter stock expensive relative to other options and consignment resented with difficult collections.
For outside circulation, route inquiries to a local store rather than mailing, so the supplying dealer gains a customer.
caveats: Coupons good for full-size packages risk being bought up in bulk; the source advises avoiding announced dates and using Sunday papers.
Methods vary by line and retailer power; test in representative markets before committing.

cards.title: Don't buy dealer effort; buy customers
cards.summary: Dealer help, loading discounts and displays often shift sales between stores rather than growing total sales — spend that money on creating customers instead.
cards.use_when: Evaluating trade discounts, loading offers, display allowances and display placement as a route to sales growth.
steps: Test any dealer incentive by comparing total market sales, not sales at the promoted store: a window display may give one dealer a larger share without increasing your total.
Treat loading offers (e.g. one case free with ten) as requiring 10% more advertising-sold volume just to return the same revenue.
Recognize that most dealers push their own brands and that advertised lines carry thin margins and get price-cut, so anticipated extra effort is often not forthcoming.
Prefer sales made by conviction through advertising; Hopkins says customers won through casual recommendation rarely stick.
If you do fund display or trade promotions, compare cost per incremental customer against the equivalent spend on media that creates new buyers.
Accept that if customers cost you one dollar each, every wasted dollar is a lost customer; set this as your spend criterion.
caveats: Some categories — impulse, luxury, grocery — depend on display and shelf placement for discoverability; don't eliminate trade support without testing.
The source's argument assumes advertising is the primary demand creator, which may not hold for products without brand pull.

cards.title: Positive ads beat negative appeals
cards.summary: Show the desired outcome and the envied life, not the problem or the afflicted customer; Hopkins claims positive ads pull four to one over negative ones.
cards.use_when: Choosing imagery, headlines and proof points for ads, PDP hero images or landing pages for beauty, health, apparel, education or self-improvement products.
steps: Replace 'before' imagery with 'after' imagery: show clear skin, not wrinkles; pretty teeth, not decayed ones; well-dressed people, not shabby ones.
Do not attack rivals, point out their faults or appear to knock competitors; apart from issues of media acceptance, the selfishness is obvious and costs trust.
Write invitations rather than accusations: 'Send now for this sample' rather than 'Why do you neglect this offer?', which implies the reader is already neglecting.
Assume readers will act and invite them to follow the crowd.
Where relevant, include a person who benefits from the transformation — the source notes beauty advertising gains from including an admiring man, since women use beauty to gain effect.
Keep every ad cheerful in tone; Hopkins says readers dodge a lugubrious advertiser.
caveats: The four-to-one figure is Hopkins' stated experience, not a general benchmark; test against your own audience.
Some categories respond to honest problem agitation; the source concedes negative appeals may work with 'the afflicted' and for remedies.

cards.title: Keep a consistent advertising personality
cards.summary: Give your advertising a consistent, distinctive personality and don't change what has proved appealing; readers build confidence through repeated acquaintance.
cards.use_when: Setting tone of voice for an ongoing campaign and onboarding new writers or agencies who produce ad and PDP copy.
steps: Choose an individuality suited to the audience: rugged honesty where it counts, good-fellow tone where choice is a matter of favour, or authority where technical confidence is needed.
Attribute responsibility where possible — name the person who made an improvement or sign the ads — so a face rather than a soulless corporation speaks.
Give each writer your established tone before they draft: Hopkins says a new writer 'gets into the spirit adopted' and plays the part like an actor.

Never change an individuality that has proved appealing; readers recognize you by mannerisms as much as name, and appearing different every time undermines trust, forcing best friends to reacquaint themselves.
Allow a complete change only when a wrong approach forces it.
If you change, don't force traits that conflict with your audience's preferences; be distinctive without becoming eccentric or abnormal.
caveats: Consistency must not preserve a tone that a new test has disproven; the source permits a complete change when the tack is wrong.
Signed ads require the named person to be credible and available; otherwise the device backfires.

cards.title: Make pictures argue only when letters wouldn't pay better
cards.summary: Pictures are often a third to a half of the campaign stake, so use them only when they out-sell the same space in type, and never merely to attract attention.
cards.use_when: Allocating space between imagery and copy in ads or on PDP and landing pages, and deciding art style.
steps: Before commissioning any image, ask whether the same space as persuasive type would sell more; if not, use type.

Use pictures to make a selling argument type can't make: products whose appearance drives desire (clothing, collars, food), or aspirational figures (successful men for business courses, admired women for beauty).
Test rather than assume — the source cites grains photographs beating figure drawings for one product and other pictures being a total loss.
Avoid eccentric, comic or frivolous imagery: it steals attention from the headline and appeal, and Hopkins argues no one patronizes a clown.

On art quality and colour, treat these as minor economies: good art pays at least as well as mediocre; colour generally pays only where it approximates the product (orange, desserts), not merely to attract attention.
Repeat a proven picture rather than replacing it: Hopkins argues new customers won't remember it, so repetition is an economy.
caveats: The 'third to a half of campaign stake' refers to space cost in print advertising; digital equivalents differ.
Art quality and colour questions have both viewpoints supported in the source and depend on the line and modern media.

cards.title: Test copy letters like ads before sending at scale
cards.summary: Write and test multiple letters as you would ads; a letter reaching a half-sold prospect can either complete the sale or forfeit the impression.
cards.use_when: Designing follow-up emails, direct mail or outreach to prospects and previous buyers for an ecommerce list.
steps: Analyse which circular letters you personally act on or file; the ones that survive have a headline offering something you want or need to know, at a glance.
Recognise that half-sold prospects are the highest-value recipients: letters to inquirers and follow-ups complete a sale or forfeit the impression gained, so they matter as much as the original ad.
Before sending millions, send a few thousand split across many variants — one publisher tested 25 letters to a thousand prospects each — and learn which produces the best result.
Use the variant with the best measured returns; abandon a plan that tests unprofitable rather than rolling it out.
Where testing at scale isn't possible, base the letter on knowledge gained from prior tests, not assumptions.
Apply the same test-different-copy discipline to ad creative and landing pages, not just letters.
caveats: Assumes a list or inquiry base large enough to split into meaningful test cells.
The source is pre-digital; modern email and deliverability constraints change cadence but not the test-before-scale principle.

cards.title: Eliminate costs that don't produce measurable sales
cards.summary: Weigh every project and method against a known cost per result, because small economies are irrelevant next to basic appeals that can halve or multiply results.
cards.use_when: Auditing any campaign spend — dealer allowances, displays, samples, art, media — and deciding where to cut or reallocate budget.
steps: Identify the few variables that can halve or multiply results — the appeal, the headline, the offer — and treat art quality, colour, specific ad details and dealer perks as minor economies.
For every spend line, run a comparison test: some towns with the treatment, some without, and compare total sales, not just sales at promoted outlets.
Note that questions can be settled cheaply by a test campaign rather than by argument; Hopkins calls it going to the court of last resort — buyers.

Estimate whether an effort is too costly in advance: if converting a habit or reaching a tiny minority means a per-customer cost that can't be repaid from the customer's lifetime spend, don't attempt it.
Consider that what can't be done profitably on a large scale usually can't be done on a small scale either; partial funding of a losing objective is the same folly, smaller.
Apply the same criteria you use for manufacturing costs to advertising, so every element is compared on cost and result.
caveats: Some brand and awareness spending is not immediately measurable; don't cut everything without a measurable return if you have strategic reasons and can measure over a longer horizon.
The source assumes a mail-order measurement framework; adapt the method to the measurement tools your channel supports.
